content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This paper was reviewed by three experts in the field. The AC and reviewers had a thorough discussion on this paper, where the reviewers raised many concerns regarding the paper: 1) The technical contribution is relatively marginal compared to previous works such as [19]. 2) The proposed method is inferior in dealing with identity preservation. Considering the reviewers' concerns, we regret that the paper cannot be recommended for acceptance at this time. The authors are encouraged to consider the reviewers' comments when revising the paper for submission elsewhere.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Though this paper has presented a complete system for talking head generation, most of the proposed modules did not constitute significant technical contributions.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting: During the AC-reviewer discussion, the reviewers first acknowledged the additional experiments provided in the rebuttal. However, the reviewers raised two major concerns regarding the paper: 1) The technical contribution is relatively marginal compared to previous works such as [19]. 2) The proposed method is inferior in dealing with identity preservation.

content.title: Thank you for author's response
content.comment:
I thank the author for their detailed response, and I sincerely apologize for my late reply.

I am satisfied with the response from the author about my concerns. I understand the design of the method and key contributions better after reading the explanation. I appreciate the author updated the figures with consideration of my suggestions. After reading other reviews and author's response, I think the author improved the current paper with these additional experiments and clarifications. 

My main concern remains as the contribution over previous works [19] is the facial meta-memory bank, which is not strong. I know it is a very subjective judgment that I do not think the current paper is an exciting ICLR paper. Therefore, I would like to remain my current rating while raising the Correctness part to be "well-supported and correct".

content.title: Response to Reviewer StKu
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and insightful comments. We address the questions and comments below. 
>R3.Q1: More explanation of the "scale conditioned" of the model.

Thank the reviewer for the comment. We give more elaboration about this point here. Our model learns a global facial meta-memory bank from the entire training face dataset for source feature compensation, which is the major contribution of this work. Learning the scale-aware implicit representation from the source is an additional contribution for us to better utilize the global meta-memory bank. We explain more about the motivation and details as follows. 

The facial meta-memory bank contains facial representations with different scales, which can be observed from the visualization of the different channels of the meta-memory (see Figure 7, Figure 9, and Figure 10), as the training data consists of facial image samples with different scales. Each input source image also has a specific face scale. We aim to query the global meta-memory bank to obtain facial representations that are consistent with the scale of the input source, which is then used to perform feature compensation for the source. This is the reason why we need to have a scale conditioned on the input source for the query of the global meta-memory. 

To achieve this goal, we utilize the face-keypoint coordinates of the input source images. They are normalized on the same 2D image plane for all the input images, thus essentially containing scale information of the face of the source image. The normalized face-keypoint coordinates are then fed into an MLP to learn a scale representation of the source face. As the input is normalized coordinates, the representation of the face scale is thus considered to be implicit. 

It should be noted that we are not using the implicit-scale representations to perform scaling on the source. Instead, we use the learned implicit-scale representation from MLP to predict weights for us to query the global meta-memory, as discussed in Sec. 3.2. As the convolutional weights predicted from the implicit scale representation can decide which channels of the global metra memory will be used more (larger weight values) for the current input source, the query of the global meta-memory bank is input-source-scale conditioned. The query finally produces a scale-aware memory bank, which is used for the compensation of the warped source feature map. 

Moreover, we show the ablation studies on different datasets and illustrate more qualitative results (see Table 5, Table 6, Figure 11 and Figure 12 in the Appendix) to further verify the effectiveness of our implicit scale representation.

>R3.Q2: Explanation of some parts of the method.

Thank the reviewer for the comments. In the generation stage, we perform warping of the source feature map from different network layers. These source feature maps thus have different spatial resolutions. The large-resolution feature map contains more facial details, while higher resolution one contains more semantic information of the face. This multi-layer warping is typically carried out in previous existing works such as TPSM. Then, it is straightforward for us to perform the memory compensation with the learned global mete-memory bank for each resolution source feature map, thus being able to capture more details of the facial face in the generation. 

Regarding the warped feature compensation, it is our design and is directly related to our contribution. We query the global meta-memory to obtain a scale-aware memory bank for the current input source image. Then, we use the scale-aware memory bank to compensate for the warped feature map obtained from applying the motion field estimated from the target on the source feature map. The warped feature map contains ambiguity for generation because of large motion or occlusion. 

>R3.Q3: Minor comments and codes for reproducibility.

Thank the reviewer for the suggestion. Regarding a better visualization of the learned meta-memory, we show both reduced channels in a larger and more clear view (see Figure 9) and all the channels in a full view (see Figure 10). For better visualisation, we put some channel samples in high resolution in the Appendix of the rebuttal revision. 

Regarding motion estimation, we use the same motion estimation method as in FOMM and DaGAN. We have modified the text to make this point more clear. 

Regarding reproducibility, we will release the code and trained models once the paper is accepted to benefit the community.

content.title: Response to Reviewer gGqi
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and insightful comments. We address the questions and comments below. 

>R2.Q1: A comparison with FOMM, MRAA, and TPSN in a different image animation domain.

Thank the reviewer for the comment. FOMM, MRAA, and TPSN all conducted experiments on the talking head generation task, and released their checkpoints publicly. As the setup and evaluation protocol is the same for all the methods, the advantage of our model compared to the previous state-of-the-art methods on the talking head generation is solid as shown in Table 1 in the paper. 

Table: Result comparison on TED-talks dataset.
| Model | $\mathcal{L}_1$$\downarrow$ | (AKD $\downarrow$ , MKR $\downarrow$ )| AED$\downarrow$ | 
|---|---|---|---|
FOMM | 0.033| (7.07, 0.014) | 0.163
MRAA  |0.026| (4.01, 0.012) | 0.116 
TPSM  |0.027|(3.39, 0.007)| 0.124
Ours    |0.023|(2.52, 0.006)| 0.101

Following the suggestion of the reviewer, we also perform another image animation task, which is human-body video generation on a widely used dataset, i.e., the TED-talks dataset. It contains videos of TED talks downloaded from youtube. The resolution of the videos for the task is 384*384 with the upper parts of human bodies. We follow the same experimental setup of the previous methods and report the comparison with the state-of-the-arts in the table above (also shown in Table 8 in the Appendix). It can be clearly observed that our method can still achieve the best results compared to all the competitors, on the AKD, MKR, and AED metrics, which are the same metrics used in the previous methods. This experiment confirms the generalization capability of our model to other image animation tasks, in which large poses and occlusions in videos also commonly exist.

>R2.Q2: The proposed implicit scale conditioned memory module (ISCM) learns implicit scale representation which is hard to visualize or compare to show its effect.

Thank the reviewer for the comment. As can be observed from Table 2, ISCM indeed obtains consistent improvements on the different image-quality-related metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS and $\mathcal{L}_1$). More significantly, for the face-reenactment-related metrics (i.e., AKD and AED), ISCM achieves relatively larger improvements. We also want to mention that the improvements of ISCM are based on a very strong baseline model we built, which already outperforms most of the state-of-the-art models, and is very competitive with the best-performing method TPSM. Thus, the improvements of ISCM are very solid. Moreover, we also report the results of ablation studies on two new datasets, i.e., Voxceleb2 and HDTF (see Table 5 and Table 6 in the Appendix or tables shown in the next question). The results show that the ISCM can also bring very clear improvements on these two datasets. It verifies the effectiveness of our designed ISCM. Moreover, we present more qualitative ablation results in Figure 11 and Figure 12 in the Appendix to further demonstrate the effectiveness of ISCM.

>R2.Q3: Evaluation on new datasets.

Thank the reviewer for the suggestion. To further verify our method, we evaluate and compare our MCNet with the state-of-the-art methods on VoxCeleb2 and HDTF datasets. The results are shown below, and also included in the Appendix of the revised revision (see Table 5 and Table 6). It can be observed that our method also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on these two new datasets, further demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed model.

Table: Result comparison on VoxCeleb2.

content.title: Response to Reviewer dF7D
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and insightful comments. We address the questions and comments below. 

>R1.Q1: Can this method scale to high-resolution images?

Thank the reviewer for the comments. In this work, we aim to learn a global meta memory from the entire training dataset, to represent facial appearance and structure knowledge, for facial compensation in the talking head video generation. Because we adopt an encoder-decoder architecture for our generator, it is flexible for us to modify the architecture to adapt the training on high-resolution images. 

>R1.Q2: Would the facial details be a challenge to learn with this method?

The target of our proposal is to provide better facial generation details, through the learning and utilization of the global facial meta-memory. It can effectively compensate for facial ambiguities in generation caused by large facial poses and occlusions, which produce artifacts in the facial details and downgrade the quality of generated facial images. Extensive experiments show that our approach can achieve better generation results compared with the previous state-of-the-art methods, as shown in the quantitative comparison in Table 1, and the qualitative comparison in Figure 5 in the main paper. 

>R1.Q3: Ablation study on identity preservation

Following the suggestion of the reviewer, we reorganize the voxceleb1 dataset and divide it into a training set and a test set. These two sets have the same identity space. That is, the identities of test videos also appear in the training videos. We select 500 videos as the test set and the rest as the training set. The experimental results are shown below. We can observe that our method achieves higher performance under the setting of testing identity as a part of the training corpus. One possible reason is that our global meta-memory is learned from the identities in the entire training set. In this way, it can better compensate for the facial details of these seen identities.

|Model|SSIM (%) $\uparrow$  | PSNR $\uparrow$ | LPIPS$\downarrow$ |$\mathcal{L}_1$$\downarrow$ |AKD$\downarrow$ | AED$\downarrow$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
Identities not in the training set| 82.5| 31.94| 0.174|0.0331|1.203|0.106
Identities in the training set| 83.6| 32.38|0.163|0.0319|1.164|0.102

>R1.Q4: More elaboration on the ablation study of the proposed architectural designs.

Thank the reviewer for the comment. The comprehensive ablation study is shown in Table 2. As we can observe from Table 2, our different components achieve clear improvements on all six metrics (i.e., SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, L1, AKD, and AED), in which the first four metrics measure the quality of the generated images, and the last two metrics reflect the fidelity of face-reenactment. Notably, our model produces significant improvement over the baseline on the SSIM (82.5 vs 81.1), LPIPS (1.303 vs. 1.203,), and AED (0.124 vs. 0.106) metrics. These improvements are not trivial, considering that our baseline model is already very strong, which outperforms most of the state-of-the-art models, and is very competitive with the best-performing method TPSM. Besides, we plugged our model into different state-of-the-art methods, including FOMM and TPSM. Our model can further boost their performances on all the metrics, which is a strong evidence of the effectiveness of our model. All of these experimental results can fully demonstrate the proposed model. Besides, we also show the qualitative results of different ablation studies in Figure 6. We can observe consistently improved generation performances from different components of our model. Moreover, we show more qualitative ablation results in Figure11 and Figure12 in the Appendix to further verify the effectiveness of each component of our method. 


>R1.Q5: Some inconsistency or typos on identity-independent and scale-aware memory bank, and codes for Reproducibility.

Thank the reviewer for pointing it out. Our global meta-memory back is identity independent, as it is learned from the entire dataset. While the scale-aware memory bank is generated by the query of the global facial meta-memory, using the source-specific keypoints as a condition. The queried scale-aware memory bank is then used for feature compensation for the corresponding input source. We are sorry for the typos, and we have made them consistent in the revised version. Regarding the project code, we will release the code and trained models to benefit the community upon the paper’s acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presented a method for learning talking head generation/reenactment. Specifically, the paper proposed a memory bank based architecture to address the inconsistency caused by varying shape/appearance of source and driving signals. A learnable external prior is introduced to learn and store the shape/appearance coupling. Some other modules and architectural designs are also proposed in the paper to improve the performance of the method, specifically handling the scale difference between source and driving signals. The paper provided qualitative and quantitative comparisons with some existing approaches, including, FOMM, DaGAN, TPSM etc. The proposed method achieves better performance on image quality and identity preservation, albeit with relatively small margin. The paper also provided quantitative ablation study to demonstrate the effectiveness of each component.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The problem that the paper is aiming to address is interesting and is an essential challenge in face reenactment work. Keypoint and warping based method for transferring dynamic facial appearance often suffers from inconsistency between the driving signals and target image, especially in terms of shape and scale of the images.

2. The approach is novel to me by leveraging a memory bank as a global face appearance representation and use it for a face reenactment task.

3. The experimental results demonstrated the advantage of the proposed method. The qualitative results in the paper and supplemental video showed clear advantage over previous work. The quantitative performances on image quality and identity preservation evaluation also outperformed previous work.


Weaknesses:

No major concern from me except a few minor questions:

1. Can this method scale to very high resolution images? Would the facial details be challenge or too expensive to learn with this method?

2. The method seems still have issue with identity preservation, which is a common issue in such tasks. Since the method is learning a memory bank from training data, would it make any difference if the testing identity is a part of the training corpus? Perhaps an ablation study on identity preservation could help explain.

 2. Ablation study. The network design is quite complicated, which is my major concern with this paper. I'm not sure how much of them could be simplified. It is good that the author provided the ablation study to show the accumulating benefit of each component, but it's a little disappointing that each of which doesn't seem to contribute much upon the baseline. More importantly, there seem to be lack of qualitative comparisons for the ablation study. How much difference can we see in the results by adding the proposed architectural designs?

Some inconsistency or typos:

- In section 3.1, the paper refer Ms as " identity-independent scale-aware memory bank Ms". But in section 3.2, last paragraph, the paper stated "person-dependent scale-aware memory Ms" which is the direct opposite of the early statement. Is there a typo or am I missing something?

- Section 3.2 last paragraph, "scale-dependent scale-aware memory bank Ms" -- why mention scale twice? Perhaps a typo?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work seems to be original and the paper is overall easy to read. The architecture design and the motivations of it are both well documented and explained in the text. The experiments are also clear to me. Overall I think the quality and clarity are good.
content.summary_of_the_review: I appreciate the motive, method, and results of the paper. I have some complaints about the method being complicated and might be challenge to reproduce (I hope the code and model will be published alongside the paper). I also have some minor questions/suggestions about the paper as mentioned above. Overall I'm positive on this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new video-driven talking head generation method based on memory band learning and implicit scale representation learning. The proposed model, named as MCNet, consists of:
1) a keypoint detector and the dense motion network that predicts keypoints from source and driving frame and then estimates optical flow between them,
2) an implicit scale conditioned module ISCM that encodes implicit scale representation from warped feature and source keypoints, which is then conditioned on the query of the meta memory to produce identity-independent scale-aware memory band,
3) a memory compensation module MCM that utilizes a dynamic cross-attention mechanism to spatially compensate the warped features, which is finally produced into final image by decoder.
The MCNet learns global facial meta memory bank to obtain global facial priors on spatial structure and appearance from all available training faces and compensate for dynamic facial synthesis, addressing the ambiguities in face generation especially in situation of large head pose change.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The paper proposes to learn a global facial meta memory bank to transfer representative facial representations to handle the appearance and structure ambiguities caused by the highly dynamic generation from a still source image
+ The paper proposes an implicit scale conditioned memory module (ISCM) to learn implicit scale representation from warped feature and source keypoints and addresses the problem that different source faces contain distinct scales.
+ The paper proposes a memory compensation module (MCM) to compensate and refine the warped feature map, which utilized the learned global prior facial information to generate better results.
+ The qualitative and quantitative comparisons to STOA in both same-identity reenactment and cross-identity reenactment show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
+ Ablation studies are conducted to visualize the learned meta memory and show the effectiveness of each module.

Weaknesses:
- The method is proposed as a talking head generation method, but many compared SOTA methods such as FOMM, MRAA and TPSN are general image animation methods capable of animating images from different domains, which makes the comparison with these methods in face image domain somehow less convincing.
- The proposed implicit scale conditioned memory module (ISCM) learns implicit scale representation which is hard to visualize or compare to show its effect, and the quantitative results of the ablation study show that the ISCM module has only very slightly improvement on the evaluation metrics.
- The evaluation datasets are not sufficient. It’s better to perform experiment on some new datasets such as VoxCeleb2 and high-resolution dataset HDTF.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This work has high quality and the idea and framework are clear. It is innovative and is able to be reproduced according to the details provided in the appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a novel method based on good observation of human face and effectively improves the performance of facial reenactment.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new talking head generation method with memory compensation. The proposed method is novel with good experiment performances. The claimed implicitly scale condition is confusing, however, it could be addressed by editing the paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The proposed method is novel in terms of using the meta memory bak to transfer representative facial representations. Compared to the previous works [19], the main novelty comes from the memory module and compensation module. The two modules are reasonable to me and the author has clearly demonstrated their implementation of them. 

- The method is well demonstrated. The author has provided three figures Fig. 2, 3, 4 to demonstrate the architecture of the proposed method with detailed text. The proposed method is a bit complex, and I hope the author could release their source code upon acceptance. The author provides the visualization of the meta memory to show the learned memory content.

- The proposed method achieves the best performance on two datasets for both same-identity reenactment and cross-identity reenactment experiments. The author also provides a detailed ablation study to show the benefit of meta-memory learning, scale-aware memory learning etc.

Weakness:
- It is not clear to me why the author claims "scale" conditioned. First, the author motivated the scale is important because adults and children have different face scales (beginning of section 3.2). However, there are no children in the data that they tested on. I do not understand why the author cares about the scale in this case. Second, there is no evaluation to show that the proposed method indeed implicitly learns the "scale" although the ablation study shows the scale module can improve the performance. I do not think the author could claim they have the "implicit scale representation". Last, the implementation of the scale is scaling of the convolutional weights, which is not the scale of the face. I do not think scaling the weights has the semantic meaning of scaling the face. Taken together, I am confused why the author focuses on the scale in this proposed method rather than the meta memory.

- There are many parts of the method without an explanation of why the author does that. For example, the multi-layer generation in section 3.3 is upsampling operations that claim to "preserve the details of the face", which is not clear to me why and how. The Wrapped facial feature compensation has similar issues that I do not see why the author has this specific architectural design. Is that the author designed the module from the scratch by themselves, or did the author borrow this module from previous works (for which I did not see the citation)?


Minor comments:
- The images in Fig. 7 are too small to see and zooming in just ends up with blurry images. I suggest the author reduce the number of meta memory in Fig. 7 to have a better visualisation.
- The author writes "Specifically, compared with FOMM and DaGAN, which adopt the same motion estimation method as ours ...". Does it mean the author takes their proposed method as a motion estimation method? I think the meta memory is the main character of the method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper writing is clear, although there are some minor parts that could be improved. The proposed method is novel. Although the author provides a detailed description of the method, I think the source code is still needed to re-produce the same results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is novel and achieves the best performance on two datasets. There are some issues in this paper that could be addressed by re-writing part of the paper.

content.title: Learning Implicit Scale Conditioned Memory Compensation for Talking Head Generation
content.TL;DR: We propose a novel implicit scale conditioned memory compensation network (MCNet) for high-fidelity talking head generation.
content.abstract: Talking head video generation aims to animate the pose and expression of a person in a target driving video using motion information contained in the video, while maintaining a person's identity in a given still source image. Highly dynamic and complex motions in the driving video cause ambiguous generation from the source image, because the still source image cannot provide sufficient appearance information for occluded regions or delicate expressions, which severely produces artifacts and significantly degrades the generation quality. However, existing works mainly focus on learning more accurate motion estimation and representation in 2D and 3D, and they ignore the facial structural prior in addressing the facial ambiguities. Therefore, effective handling of the ambiguities in the dramatic appearance changes of the source to largely improve facial details and completeness in generation still remains barely explored. To this end, we propose a novel implicit scale conditioned memory compensation network (MCNet) for high-fidelity talking head generation. Specifically, considering human faces are symmetric and structured, we aim to automatically learn a representative global facial memory bank from all training data as a prior to compensate for the facial generation features. Each face in the source image contains a scale that can be reflected in detected facial keypoints. To better query the learned global memory, we further propose to learn implicit scale representations from the discrete keypoints, which can be used to condition on the query of the global memory, to obtain scale-aware memory for the feature compensation. Extensive experiments from quantitative and qualitative perspectives demonstrate that MCNet can learn representative and complementary facial memory, and can clearly outperform previous state-of-the-art methods on VoxCeleb1 and CelebV datasets.
